output.name: Tilsa
output.myth: When the ice goes out of the bays, the old women take the nets down from the cliff poles. The mending-thread goes back onto the shuttle, and the shuttle goes in and out of the holes, under and over, the way wind goes round a sail. Ennu the Kite-Wright carved the first one from a goat's shoulder-blade and taught the women the knot. Aun saw it in spring and asked to borrow it. He ran the thread through every hole in the sky and lost the end past the Cut Kite, out to the south-east, where he still holds the knife. Hesk the Reel counted what came back and found it short by one thread's length. So the Shuttle rises at the thaw, facing the Bridled Kite in the north-east, which keeps its one knot for the wind to pull against. Ránu streams behind to the south, its ribbon still loose. The old women say, when the net is mended, the sky is mended too, and the fish come in. Hesk does not forgive, but she counts.
output.finding: Find the Bridled Kite in the north-east, then sight about a fist and a half (14°) south-west of it, where the Shuttle rises at the thaw.
